28:27.ar: قَالَ إِنِّيٓ أُرِيدُ أَنۡ أُنكِحَكَ إِحۡدَى ٱبۡنَتَيَّ هَٰتَيۡنِ عَلَىٰٓ أَن تَأۡجُرَنِي ثَمَٰنِيَ حِجَجࣲۖ فَإِنۡ أَتۡمَمۡتَ عَشۡرࣰ ا فَمِنۡ عِندِكَۖ وَمَآ أُرِيدُ أَنۡ أَشُقَّ عَلَيۡكَۚ سَتَجِدُنِيٓ إِن شَآءَ ٱللَّهُ مِنَ ٱلصَّٰلِحِينَ
28:27.en: He said: Lo! I fain would marry thee to one of these two daughters of mine on condition that thou hirest thyself to me for (the term of) eight pilgrimages. Then if thou completest ten it will be of thine own accord, for I would not make it hard for thee. Allah willing, thou wilt find me of the righteous

28:28.ar: قَالَ ذَٰلِكَ بَيۡنِي وَبَيۡنَكَۖ أَيَّمَا ٱلۡأَجَلَيۡنِ قَضَيۡتُ فَلَا عُدۡوَٰنَ عَلَيَّۖ وَٱللَّهُ عَلَىٰ مَا نَقُولُ وَكِيلࣱ‏
28:28.en: He said: That (is settled) between thee and me. Whichever of the two terms I fulfil, there will be no injustice to me, and Allah is Surety over what we say

28:29.ar: ۞فَلَمَّا قَضَىٰ مُوسَى ٱلۡأَجَلَ وَسَارَ بِأَهۡلِهِۦٓ ءَانَسَ مِن جَانِبِ ٱلطُّورِ نَارࣰ اۖ قَالَ لِأَهۡلِهِ ٱمۡكُثُوٓاْ إِنِّيٓ ءَانَسۡتُ نَارࣰ ا لَّعَلِّيٓ ءَاتِيكُم مِّنۡهَا بِخَبَرٍ أَوۡ جَذۡوَةࣲ مِّنَ ٱلنَّارِ لَعَلَّكُمۡ تَصۡطَلُونَ
28:29.en: Then, when Moses had fulfilled the term, and was travelling with his housefolk, he saw in the distance a fire and said unto his housefolk: Bide ye (here). Lo! I see in the distance a fire; peradventure I shall bring you tidings thence, or a brand from the fire that ye may warm yourselves

2:30.ar: وَإِذۡ قَالَ رَبُّكَ لِلۡمَلَٰٓئِكَةِ إِنِّي جَاعِلࣱ فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِ خَلِيفَةࣰۖ قَالُوٓاْ أَتَجۡعَلُ فِيهَا مَن يُفۡسِدُ فِيهَا وَيَسۡفِكُ ٱلدِّمَآءَ وَنَحۡنُ نُسَبِّحُ بِحَمۡدِكَ وَنُقَدِّسُ لَكَۖ قَالَ إِنِّيٓ أَعۡلَمُ مَا لَا تَعۡلَمُونَ
2:30.en: And when thy Lord said unto the angels: Lo! I am about to place a viceroy in the earth, they said: Wilt thou place therein one who will do harm therein and will shed blood, while we, we hymn Thy praise and sanctify Thee? He said: Surely I know that which ye know not

CH7C2iSPx9g.title: A Decade in London: 10 Reflection Points
CH7C2iSPx9g.one_line: On his tenth anniversary in London, ten personal lessons: stay with Allah, play your hand, purpose, grit, time, relationships, opinions, death, uncertainty and love.
CH7C2iSPx9g.summary: He notes that Musa spent a decade in Madyan and the Prophet ten years each in Makkah and Madinah, then reflects on the ten years since he arrived in London during Ramadan with his life reset to nothing. He offers ten individual lessons rather than institutional ones. Stay with Allah in good times and bad, since He never leaves and everything else changes. All that is expected is the best you can do with the hand you hold now, as he sees with oncology patients whose lives change in a day. Fulfillment needs purpose and companionship, the two things Adam was given. If you are doing the right thing with the right tools, be relentless like the Prophet, because you only lose when you stay down. Time is your only real currency, so guard it. In the second half he urges managing relationships by drawing close to people who bring you nearer to Allah and treasuring like-minded friends. People think about you far less than you fear. Accept death early, because it makes life brighter. Feeling lost or afraid is normal, even the Prophet felt fear, but decide and move on. Love is your most valuable possession, so give it wisely. None of his own ten-year plans came true, and that is fine.

outline.heading: Opening
The meaning of a decade: Musa and the Prophet
outline.gist: Musa left Egypt for Madyan, agreed to serve eight or ten years, completed ten and received revelation on the way back. The companions summarized the Prophet's mission the same way: ten years in Makkah and ten in Madinah.

outline.heading: Ten years of rebuilding, ten individual lessons
outline.gist: He landed in London in Ramadan ten years ago feeling someone had pressed reset on his life, and after months of reflection offers ten lessons on the individual level, not the institutional one, especially for the young.

outline.heading: Point one: stay with Allah
outline.gist: Stay with Allah for better or worse; the bond with the Creator is closer than a parent's with a child. He never left you; everything and everyone else changes and leaves, and even after sins there is nowhere to go but back to Him.

outline.heading: Point two: do the best with the hand you hold
outline.gist: All that is expected is the best you can do with your present reality, which changes constantly. Do not dwell on what might have been; his oncology patients are dealt a completely different hand in a single day.

outline.heading: Point three: purpose and companionship
outline.gist: Fulfillment needs both, the two things Allah gave Adam: khalifah as his purpose and a spouse. Without knowing why you are alive something eats away at you, however rich you are; Allah has told you who you are and where you are going.

outline.heading: Point four: be relentless
outline.gist: If you are doing the right thing with the right tools, have more grit than anyone; every failure is a building brick. The Prophet's relentlessness is the trait he most admires: you only lose when you stay down. Consult others to confirm you are on the right path.

outline.heading: Point five: time is your currency
outline.gist: Money, friends and homes come and go, but time never returns; you are just time. Spend it only where and with whom it deserves to be spent. The younger generation's biggest problem is time management; seek help to learn it.

outline.heading: Interlude
Point six: manage your relationships
outline.gist: Draw close to those who bring you nearer to Allah and step back politely from those who waste your time, without hatred or cutting off unless there is abuse. A like-minded friend is a gem worth more than a job, a car or a house.

outline.heading: Point seven: people think of you far less than you fear
outline.gist: Everyone is self-centred and thinks of you only when it serves them. Social norms matter, but do not draw your self-worth from opinions; consult, then be true to yourself, since people talk for a week and move on.

outline.heading: Point eight: accept death, the earlier the better
outline.gist: Everyone is heading to a last breath. Accepting it is empowering, not depressing: the sun shines brighter and every meeting becomes an opportunity. Soon we will not even be a memory, like the great-grandfathers we never think of; teach children to accept it.

outline.heading: Point nine: it is okay to be lost or afraid
outline.gist: Confusion, fear and despair are universal; no one has it figured out, so speak to people who understand. Even the Prophet ran down the mountain in fear and made dua at Badr until the companions felt for him. Accept fragility but not weakness: decide and move forward.

outline.heading: Point ten: love is your most valuable possession
outline.gist: Give love wisely and wholeheartedly to parents, siblings, spouse, children and close friends before the chance is gone; do not confuse it with lust or chemistry. Shaytan takes it away through jealousy, hatred and arrogance, its true opposites. The Prophet's heart was full of love.

outline.heading: Interlude
Ten-year plans that never came true
outline.gist: Not one of the plans he made on landing happened, and that is fine: plan, work hard and accept a different hand. Young people in their twenties should write down who they hope to be by 2030 and work toward it.

outline.heading: Outro

Fo8O4P1gsaY.one_line: A short clip reading two hadith on Arafah, the Day of Sacrifice and the days of Tashreeq as the festival of the Muslims.
Fo8O4P1gsaY.summary: A brief Arafah-season clip. The reader narrates the hadith of Uqbah ibn Amir, reported by al-Nasa'i with a sound chain, that the Day of Arafah, the Day of Sacrifice and the days of Tashreeq are the festival of the people of Islam, days of eating and drinking, linking it to the remembrance of Allah over the livestock He provided. He then narrates the hadith of Abdullah ibn Qurt that the greatest day with Allah is the Day of Sacrifice, with the account of the camels brought to the Prophet that drew close to be slaughtered first, and the Prophet's words that whoever wishes may take a portion. The clip closes with Eid greetings and a prayer that Allah accepts people's worship.

22:26.ar: وَإِذۡ بَوَّأۡنَا لِإِبۡرَٰهِيمَ مَكَانَ ٱلۡبَيۡتِ أَن لَّا تُشۡرِكۡ بِي شَيۡـࣰٔ ا وَطَهِّرۡ بَيۡتِيَ لِلطَّآئِفِينَ وَٱلۡقَآئِمِينَ وَٱلرُّكَّعِ ٱلسُّجُودِ
22:26.en: And (remember) when We prepared for Abraham the place of the (holy) House, saying: Ascribe thou no thing as partner unto Me, and purify My House for those who make the round (thereof) and those who stand and those who bow and make prostration

22:27.ar: وَأَذِّن فِي ٱلنَّاسِ بِٱلۡحَجِّ يَأۡتُوكَ رِجَالࣰ ا وَعَلَىٰ كُلِّ ضَامِرࣲ يَأۡتِينَ مِن كُلِّ فَجٍّ عَمِيقࣲ‏
22:27.en: And proclaim unto mankind the pilgrimage. They will come unto thee on foot and on every lean camel; they will come from every deep ravine

2:197.ar: ٱلۡحَجُّ أَشۡهُرࣱ مَّعۡلُومَٰتࣱۚ فَمَن فَرَضَ فِيهِنَّ ٱلۡحَجَّ فَلَا رَفَثَ وَلَا فُسُوقَ وَلَا جِدَالَ فِي ٱلۡحَجِّۗ وَمَا تَفۡعَلُواْ مِنۡ خَيۡرࣲ يَعۡلَمۡهُ ٱللَّهُۗ وَتَزَوَّدُواْ فَإِنَّ خَيۡرَ ٱلزَّادِ ٱلتَّقۡوَىٰۖ وَٱتَّقُونِ يَٰٓأُوْلِي ٱلۡأَلۡبَٰبِ
2:197.en: The pilgrimage is (in) the well-known months, and whoever is minded to perform the pilgrimage therein (let him remember that) there is (to be) no lewdness nor abuse nor angry conversation on the pilgrimage. And whatsoever good ye do Allah knoweth it. So make provision for yourselves (Hereafter); for the best provision is to ward off evil. Therefore keep your duty unto Me, O men of understanding

3:96.ar: إِنَّ أَوَّلَ بَيۡتࣲ وُضِعَ لِلنَّاسِ لَلَّذِي بِبَكَّةَ مُبَارَكࣰ ا وَهُدࣰ ى لِّلۡعَٰلَمِينَ
3:96.en: Lo! the first Sanctuary appointed for mankind was that at Becca, a blessed place, a guidance to the peoples

2:37.ar: فَتَلَقَّىٰٓ ءَادَمُ مِن رَّبِّهِۦ كَلِمَٰتࣲ فَتَابَ عَلَيۡهِۚ إِنَّهُۥ هُوَ ٱلتَّوَّابُ ٱلرَّحِيمُ
2:37.en: Then Adam received from his Lord words (of revelation), and He relented toward him. Lo! He is the relenting, the Merciful

49:13.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلنَّاسُ إِنَّا خَلَقۡنَٰكُم مِّن ذَكَرࣲ وَأُنثَىٰ وَجَعَلۡنَٰكُمۡ شُعُوبࣰ ا وَقَبَآئِلَ لِتَعَارَفُوٓاْۚ إِنَّ أَكۡرَمَكُمۡ عِندَ ٱللَّهِ أَتۡقَىٰكُمۡۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ عَلِيمٌ خَبِيرࣱ‏
49:13.en: O mankind! Lo! We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another. Lo! the noblest of you, in the sight of Allah, is the best in conduct. Lo! Allah is Knower, Aware

6:76.ar: فَلَمَّا جَنَّ عَلَيۡهِ ٱلَّيۡلُ رَءَا كَوۡكَبࣰ اۖ قَالَ هَٰذَا رَبِّيۖ فَلَمَّآ أَفَلَ قَالَ لَآ أُحِبُّ ٱلۡأٓفِلِينَ
6:76.en: When the night grew dark upon him he beheld a star. He said: This is my Lord. But when it set, he said: I love not things that set

6:77.ar: فَلَمَّا رَءَا ٱلۡقَمَرَ بَازِغࣰ ا قَالَ هَٰذَا رَبِّيۖ فَلَمَّآ أَفَلَ قَالَ لَئِن لَّمۡ يَهۡدِنِي رَبِّي لَأَكُونَنَّ مِنَ ٱلۡقَوۡمِ ٱلضَّآلِّينَ
6:77.en: And when he saw the moon uprising, he exclaimed: This is my Lord. But when it set, he said: Unless my Lord guide me, I surely shall become one of the folk who are astray

6:78.ar: فَلَمَّا رَءَا ٱلشَّمۡسَ بَازِغَةࣰ قَالَ هَٰذَا رَبِّي هَٰذَآ أَكۡبَرُۖ فَلَمَّآ أَفَلَتۡ قَالَ يَٰقَوۡمِ إِنِّي بَرِيٓءࣱ مِّمَّا تُشۡرِكُونَ
6:78.en: And when he saw the sun uprising, he cried: This is my Lord! This is greater! And when it set he exclaimed: O my people! Lo! I am free from all that ye associate (with Him)

6:79.ar: إِنِّي وَجَّهۡتُ وَجۡهِيَ لِلَّذِي فَطَرَ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلۡأَرۡضَ حَنِيفࣰ اۖ وَمَآ أَنَا۠ مِنَ ٱلۡمُشۡرِكِينَ
6:79.en: Lo! I have turned my face toward Him Who created the heavens and the earth, as one by nature upright, and I am not of the idolaters

2:260.ar: وَإِذۡ قَالَ إِبۡرَٰهِـۧمُ رَبِّ أَرِنِي كَيۡفَ تُحۡيِ ٱلۡمَوۡتَىٰۖ قَالَ أَوَلَمۡ تُؤۡمِنۖ قَالَ بَلَىٰ وَلَٰكِن لِّيَطۡمَئِنَّ قَلۡبِيۖ قَالَ فَخُذۡ أَرۡبَعَةࣰ مِّنَ ٱلطَّيۡرِ فَصُرۡهُنَّ إِلَيۡكَ ثُمَّ ٱجۡعَلۡ عَلَىٰ كُلِّ جَبَلࣲ مِّنۡهُنَّ جُزۡءࣰ ا ثُمَّ ٱدۡعُهُنَّ يَأۡتِينَكَ سَعۡيࣰ اۚ وَٱعۡلَمۡ أَنَّ ٱللَّهَ عَزِيزٌ حَكِيمࣱ‏
2:260.en: And when Abraham said (unto his Lord): My Lord! Show me how Thou givest life to the dead, He said: Dost thou not believe? Abraham said: Yea, but (I ask) in order that my heart may be at ease. (His Lord) said: Take four of the birds and cause them to incline unto thee, then place a part of them on each hill, then call them, they will come to thee in haste, and know that Allah is Mighty, Wise

37:102.ar: فَلَمَّا بَلَغَ مَعَهُ ٱلسَّعۡيَ قَالَ يَٰبُنَيَّ إِنِّيٓ أَرَىٰ فِي ٱلۡمَنَامِ أَنِّيٓ أَذۡبَحُكَ فَٱنظُرۡ مَاذَا تَرَىٰۚ قَالَ يَٰٓأَبَتِ ٱفۡعَلۡ مَا تُؤۡمَرُۖ سَتَجِدُنِيٓ إِن شَآءَ ٱللَّهُ مِنَ ٱلصَّٰبِرِينَ
37:102.en: And when (his son) was old enough to walk with him, (Abraham) said: O my dear son, I have seen in a dream that I must sacrifice thee. So look, what thinkest thou? He said: O my father! Do that which thou art commanded. Allah willing, thou shalt find me of the steadfast

15qYZR2mVl8.title: The Journey of Hajj
15qYZR2mVl8.one_line: Hajj as a journey of discovery: its pillars and obligations in brief, then the symbolism of ihram, tawaf, sa'i, Arafah and the stoning.
15qYZR2mVl8.summary: Hajj means pilgrimage: a journey whose value lies in the process, and a search for something. Every prophet knew the first house of worship, and Allah's promise that people would come from every distant path is fulfilled in the diversity of pilgrims. He sets out the fiqh briefly: four pillars that must be done or the Hajj is incomplete, obligations whose omission requires a sacrifice, and sunnahs that cost nothing to miss, stressing that validity and acceptance are different questions. Then he turns to meaning. Ihram is a mental transition matched by a physical one; the miqat is a portal where you leave wealth, titles and status behind. The three prohibitions remove sexuality, disobedience and the urge to argue and prove superiority, so you become one among millions. The talbiyah says I am coming gladly and I owe You for letting me come. Tawaf puts you in step with a universe that circles its centre. Sa'i follows the footsteps of Hajar. Arafah stands outside the sanctuary, like a door where the guest waits, and is where Adam and Hawa found each other again, which is why the farewell sermon on equality was given there. The stoning recalls Ibrahim, who obeyed a command he could not rationalise.

outline.heading: Opening
Hajj means a journey and a search
outline.gist: Like a road trip, the value is in the journey; and a pilgrim is looking for something.

outline.heading: Every prophet knew the first house
outline.gist: Ibrahim was told to rebuild, not build; Allah promised people would come on foot and on mounts from every far path.

outline.heading: A promise fulfilled: pilgrims from everywhere
outline.gist: At Hajj you meet thriving Muslim communities from places you never knew Islam had reached.

outline.heading: Without context the rites make no sense
outline.gist: Walking around stones and throwing pebbles is empty unless you know who stood there and why.

outline.heading: The four pillars
outline.gist: Ihram, tawaf, sa'i and standing at Arafah; miss one and you remain in Hajj until you complete it. Arafah alone separates Hajj from Umrah.

outline.heading: His teacher and the pilgrim who skipped sa'i
outline.gist: The teacher turned back with him while the bus went home; education before Hajj matters.

outline.heading: Validity versus acceptance
outline.gist: Fiqh tells you whether you discharged the duty; understanding the meaning raises the chance it is accepted.

outline.heading: Obligatory acts: ihram from the miqat, nights in Mina
outline.gist: Missing an obligation leaves the Hajj valid but you owe something; schools differ in details.

outline.heading: Arafah, Muzdalifah, stoning, shaving, farewell tawaf
outline.gist: Standing till sunset is obligatory while any moment at Arafah fulfils the pillar; arriving after dawn on Eid means next year.

outline.heading: What you owe for a missed obligation
outline.gist: One sacrifice covers missed obligations; pillars have no fixed time but must be done.

outline.heading: The sunnahs of Hajj
outline.gist: Ghusl, talbiyah, uncovering the shoulder and brisk walking, praying behind Maqam Ibrahim, Zamzam and touching the Black Stone; do not elbow people for them.

outline.heading: The fiqh in a nutshell
outline.gist: Pillars invalidate if missed, obligations cost a sacrifice, sunnahs cost nothing.

outline.heading: Every mental state has its posture
outline.gist: In prayer you recite standing, submit in ruku and ask with your face on the ground.

outline.heading: Ihram: entering a state of sanctity
outline.gist: Two unsewn cloths strip away what wealth and status bought, returning you to the simple human origin.

outline.heading: The miqat as a portal
outline.gist: Like emptying your pockets at airport security, you leave your old life behind at a place and time before entering.

outline.heading: The first no: sexuality set aside
outline.gist: No sexual expression at all; you see people simply as people.

outline.heading: No disobedience, no argument
outline.gist: Arguing is a bid for superiority; you come with full obedience and no interest in correcting others.

outline.heading: Not special: blending in
outline.gist: You try to be one among millions, with no claim to more rights than those around you.

outline.heading: The meaning of the talbiyah
outline.gist: I am coming at once, gladly, and I owe You for letting me come; the companions arrived hoarse, and the Eid takbir is our substitute.

outline.heading: Go while young; take your spouse early
outline.gist: Plan Hajj like fasting and zakat, before children; in his country of origin age limits pushed it to old age.

outline.heading: Tawaf: in step with the universe
outline.gist: From atoms to galaxies everything circles a centre counterclockwise, and in tawaf so do you.

outline.heading: Repetitive movement and focus
outline.gist: Children rock while memorising and poets composed while scything; repetition brings clarity.

outline.heading: The Kaaba is your centre, not your object of worship
outline.gist: Every prayer faces the same centre; the house was rebuilt many times but the place is what matters.

outline.heading: The corners and the Multazam
outline.gist: Where the Prophet pressed himself to make dua; go in quiet months at dawn to reach it.

outline.heading: Hijr Ismail and the lock-shaped Kaaba
outline.gist: Quraysh left the semicircle out; the Prophet did not rebuild it so as not to shake people's faith; obligatory prayers are not prayed inside.

outline.heading: Sa'i: in the footsteps of Hajar
outline.gist: No man did this first; you follow a freed slave woman, one of the greatest women ever, seven lengths from Safa to Marwah.

outline.heading: Maps: haram and hill, Arafah outside
outline.gist: Distances between the sites, and why Arafah lies outside the sacred boundary.

outline.heading: Al-Shafi'i: Arafah is the door
outline.gist: You stand at the host's door pleading, are let into the courtyard, then the house; a guest of Allah does not fast.

outline.heading: Adam and Hawa reunited at Arafah
outline.gist: Expelled after one mistake and separated, they found each other again; it cost them, not you.

outline.heading: Knowing, coming together, planning
outline.gist: Arafah from knowing, Muzdalifah from drawing close, Mina from wishes; they stoned Shaytan and built the house.

outline.heading: A yearly return to our parents' footsteps
outline.gist: Like visiting a late parent's favourite place; you go to figure out why you are here and where you are going.

outline.heading: Why the farewell sermon on equality was given there
outline.gist: No one belongs to Adam more than another; at the site of our origin he declared no race above another except by taqwa.

outline.heading: Mina and the count of pebbles
outline.gist: Seventy pebbles across the days; the later stonings symbolise Ibrahim's story.

outline.heading: Ibrahim the critical thinker
outline.gist: He argued rationally with star and idol worshippers and asked how the dead are raised.

outline.heading: A command with no visible wisdom
outline.gist: Allah never commands without benefit, but had He done so we would still obey; Muslim means giving up your will for His.

outline.heading: Stoning the one who whispered
outline.gist: Shaytan came to Ibrahim, Hajar and Ismail; they drove him off and went ahead.

outline.heading: Outro

fhNYgFScvds.title: Tackling Contemporary Issues: Navigating Differences
fhNYgFScvds.one_line: First khutbah of a summer series: how Muslims in Canada should respond to LGBTQ and gender ideology, especially in schools.
fhNYgFScvds.summary: He opens a summer series on the dozen issues that keep surfacing whenever Muslims gather, and starts with the one that worries people most, LGBTQ and gender ideology, which he never names. He frames it through the Quranic category of fawahish, an umbrella for every sexual act outside marriage between a man and a woman, and insists this includes the forms Muslims have quietly tolerated, like teenage dating, since each opened door leads to the next. He then works through three questions. What do reasonable Muslims agree on: that this halal and haram is non-negotiable, as Lut declared he detested his people's deed, and that every human being deserves dignity and freedom from discrimination; holding both is entirely possible. What is at stake: a value system handed down from Adam through all the prophets, and children who are unprepared for what they meet at school while parents give immature answers. What do we want: the right to hold and voice these values without fear, and public schools that do not teach against our faith. With no full plan, he urges people to sit on school boards, build a media presence, engage legislation, and above all bring children to the masjid through the week so the community gives them social immunity. Stop complaining, he says, and take a first step.

outline.heading: Opening
A series on the issues we keep complaining about
outline.gist: He has a list of about 12 issues that come up whenever Muslims talk for ten minutes, and will tackle seven or eight over the summer. It builds on his earlier series on education and advocacy, because these conversations end in complaints and never move further.

outline.heading: The number one worry
outline.gist: One topic is far ahead of all the others: no gathering passes without it, and he has never seen anything cause so much worry in the community. He wants a discussion that leads to a solution.

outline.heading: Fawahish: the Quranic umbrella
outline.gist: Allah lists five prohibitions and the first is fawahish, an umbrella for all promiscuous sexual activity. Intimacy between husband and wife is called rafath, as in the verses on Hajj and fasting; everything outside it, however creative, is fahisha, whether open or hidden.

outline.heading: Arriving fifty years late
outline.gist: He raised this in 2016 and 2018 and was shut down both times; Muslims always arrive forty or fifty years after the laws have passed and society has settled the question. He will not use the letters and numbers, since people get cancelled, but everyone knows the topic.

outline.heading: Three questions
outline.gist: Drawing on what people bring to him rather than his own preferences, he will ask what reasonable Muslims agree on, what is at stake, and what we really want, and only then what to do. Practising Muslims differ widely in their approach.

outline.heading: Validate other Muslims' approaches
outline.gist: Your approach depends on where you were born, raised and schooled and what you have lived through. You are entitled to yours, and must not demonize or vilify a fellow Muslim whose approach differs.

outline.heading: Specific on only two things
outline.gist: In Islam everything is permitted until stated otherwise, except two things that are tightly defined: God and sexual behaviour. There is one God and no variety, and the only acceptable sexual behaviour is between a man and a woman in marriage; Muslims tolerate other forms, like a sixteen-year-old with a girlfriend, that are just as unacceptable.

outline.heading: Open the door for one and the rest follow
outline.gist: The fawahish are dominoes: none is acceptable, they lead to each other, and the West reached where it is because it accepted one it should never have accepted.

outline.heading: First agreement: the halal and haram are not negotiable
outline.gist: Reasonable Muslims agree that what Allah made halal and haram here is crystal clear, and that these behaviours harm the doer, those around him and humanity, even in this world. It is not a chip to bargain with at the table; he would believe it if he were the last person on earth, whether or not he understood why.

outline.heading: Lut: I detest what you do
outline.gist: Lut told his people he detested their deed, a word whose roots mean refusing and declining to take part; those of his household who agreed with it, even only in their minds, were not saved with the rest.

outline.heading: Second agreement: dignity for everyone
outline.gist: Everyone, however many sins they commit and however they identify, deserves dignity, respect and freedom from discrimination, just as Muslims want for themselves. A Muslim can hold both convictions at once without contradiction.

outline.heading: In Arabic
outline.gist: He continues in Arabic before moving to the second question.

outline.heading: Second question: running away does not work
outline.gist: Some families have left the country over this, which he disagrees with: run from a problem and it follows you. Stand up to it as the Prophet did, even if it is the hardest thing this generation does and its effects are not seen in your lifetime.

outline.heading: At stake: the value system of all the prophets
outline.gist: Sometimes the dominoes do not fall within a lifetime. What people feel is threatened is the value system Allah taught Adam and that Ibrahim, Musa and every prophet lived by, now treated as unwelcome or in need of refining.

outline.heading: A moral conflict is harder than tyranny
outline.gist: Political, financial and military tyranny are well defined, and many here come from places that know them; a conflict over ethics and morals is new and disorienting, as though the message of the Torah, Zabur, Injil and Quran were no longer suitable. That is why people are frightened.

outline.heading: At stake: our children
outline.gist: In Syria a parent could send a child outside all day because every adult he met shared the same basic values. Here children come back with ideas their parents have never heard of.

outline.heading: Unprepared answers lose them
outline.gist: Caught unprepared, parents give immature answers while the other narrative seems more complete, and they lose the child. Schools were once safe hours, as the Arab ministries of 'education and upbringing' assumed; now they are not.

outline.heading: Interlude
What we want: the right to our values
outline.gist: Muslims want their values validated, not shamed; an imam should not fear losing his career for stating a view based on scripture that billions follow. They want to be able to say they disagree with a behaviour without being forced to celebrate it or take pride in what they consider sinful.

outline.heading: Ashamed to have to ask
outline.gist: He is ashamed that he must stand up and ask whether it is acceptable to believe what Allah taught. This is not hate speech: Muslims fundamentally refuse violence and discrimination against anyone; they are asking for the right to authentic principles.

outline.heading: Schools that do not contradict their faith
outline.gist: Muslim children should be able to attend public schools without being taught things that contradict their faith and values. In the verse of five prohibitions, fawahish comes before shirk, which shows this is a social issue that affects everyone, believer or not.

outline.heading: How to get there: the right tables
outline.gist: Both asks are reasonable though hard to win. He has no full plan, but Muslims must be at the right tables, starting with the school board that exists for every area.

outline.heading: Media and political advocacy
outline.gist: At the board table a compromise that keeps children away from certain content is achievable; the community has the people and expertise. Muslims also need a media presence, and individuals, not charities, can engage legislators.

outline.heading: Religious freedom and a first step
outline.gist: Ask where religious freedom comes in when laws are proposed, and work to preserve faith and rights. It needs an organized effort; Muslims can differ on approach but must stop complaining and take a first step.

outline.heading: Masajid give our children immunity
outline.gist: A social problem needs a social solution: explaining things to children academically works slowly, while being among people who live these values shapes them. Bring children through the week, not only on Jumuah, and revive the masjid's social role and mentorship; move from complaining to acting.

mFwXDHmhUqA.title: Arafah Day Program: Workshop on the Farewell Sermon
mFwXDHmhUqA.one_line: A group workshop on the eight paragraphs of the Prophet's Farewell Sermon, with his commentary on the theme of each.
mFwXDHmhUqA.summary: On the day of Arafah he turns the Farewell Sermon into a study workshop. He first sets the scene: the Prophet, once driven out of Makkah, now addresses all his followers and opens by saying he may never meet them like this again, a speech he knew would outlive its audience, so every topic was chosen deliberately. Groups each read one paragraph and name its theme, then he comments. The paragraphs he draws out are: the sanctity of life, wealth and honour, holier than Arafah itself, so harming a person is worse than sinning in Makkah; the abolition of jahiliyyah, with the Prophet forgiving his own family's blood claim and riba first, so the community could move on from its past; Shaytan's contentment with small, normalized sins once idolatry is gone; the authenticity and unity of the ummah, and the warning not to turn on each other; the rights of spouses, with men specifically told to fear Allah regarding women; human equality, where only hidden taqwa distinguishes people; the Prophet waiting at his Basin; and taking only one's due, conveying the message onward, and the haunting question of what we will say about him. He asks people to reread the sermon each Hajj season and live its values.

outline.heading: From exile to addressing the whole ummah
outline.gist: The Prophet who once spoke to a handful and was driven out of Makkah now speaks freely to all his followers.

outline.heading: 'I may never meet you again': the Prophet's farewell hints
outline.gist: He opened by saying this was likely his last address, as he had hinted in the weeks before, including to Mu'adh before Yemen.

outline.heading: Completion of the religion and Umar's tears
outline.gist: When 5:3 was revealed Umar wept, knowing nothing follows completion but decline: a sign the Prophet's mission was ending.

outline.heading: Eight carefully chosen topics
outline.gist: A brilliant speaker addressing his largest audience, relayed by riders, chose each word with no filler; read the paragraphs for their underlying idea.

outline.heading: Interlude
Paragraph one: the sanctity of life, wealth and honour
outline.gist: He reads the passage on the sacred day, month and land; groups present it as the sanctity of each person.

outline.heading: A person is more sacred than Arafah
outline.gist: Amid all that holiness, the Prophet said each person is more sacred; harming anyone is worse than sinning in the Haram, and he took Allah as witness he had told them.

outline.heading: Paragraph two: groups on blood vengeance and riba
outline.gist: Groups read it as forgiveness and the end of jahiliyyah injustice in blood and wealth, led by the Prophet's own example.

outline.heading: Jahiliyyah under his feet: moving past the past
outline.gist: He forgave the blood of his cousin Rabi'ah and his uncle Abbas's riba first; a community cannot advance while caught in its past, and this gave Islam its momentum.

outline.heading: Paragraph three: groups on being wary of sin
outline.gist: Groups name the theme as avoiding sin and what leads to it.

outline.heading: Shaytan is content with lesser sins
outline.gist: Having lost the battle over idolatry, Shaytan works on envy, insincerity and arrogance to empty deeds of value.

outline.heading: Normalizing a small sin over decades
outline.gist: Shaytan patiently lets a small sin settle for fifteen years until it no longer bothers you, then pushes the next step.

outline.heading: Paragraph four: groups on the sacred months
outline.gist: Groups discuss conduct in the sacred months and the warning against fighting each other after his death.

outline.heading: Authenticity and unity of the ummah
outline.gist: Time returning to its original order means Islam restores what Allah intended; 'do not return as kuffar' means do not put on armour against each other.

outline.heading: Paragraph five: groups on spousal rights
outline.gist: Groups outline the mutual rights of husbands and wives.

outline.heading: The final request: treat women well
outline.gist: He gave a full paragraph to spouses and addressed men alone, because it is men who need the reminder; mistreating women goes against his last advice.

outline.heading: Paragraph six: groups on racism
outline.gist: Groups present the oneness of humanity and the Abu Dharr incident.

outline.heading: Human equality and hidden taqwa
outline.gist: No one belongs to Adam more than another; taqwa is the only distinction and it is unseen, so no one can rank people; words prepared for a multicultural ummah.

outline.heading: Paragraph seven: groups on following his path
outline.gist: Groups describe the Prophet's love for his ummah and their responsibility to follow.

outline.heading: Meet me at the Basin
outline.gist: He waits at his Basin and wants to be proud of his followers; do not make him hear that you deviated.

outline.heading: Paragraph eight: groups on inheritance and lineage
outline.gist: Groups discuss taking only one's inheritance, honesty about lineage, and conveying the message.

outline.heading: Take only your right and convey the message
outline.gist: Be righteous and truthful; pass the message on, since later listeners may understand it more deeply, as equality resonates more in a global Hajj today.

outline.heading: 'You will be asked about me'
outline.gist: The Prophet asked what they would say about him; the companions wept and testified he had conveyed it, and he took Allah as witness.

outline.heading: Timeless lessons of the sermon
outline.gist: He recaps the themes and urges rereading the sermon every Hajj season.

outline.heading: Outro

hadith.gist: The Farewell Sermon: 'Listen to me, for I may not meet you after this year in this place.'
The Prophet told Mu'adh when sending him to Yemen that he might return to find only his mosque and grave, and told him not to cry.
Your blood, wealth and honour are as sacred as this day, this month and this land.
All matters of jahiliyyah are under my feet; the first blood I abolish is Rabi'ah's, the first riba that of Abbas.
Shaytan has despaired of being worshipped in this land but is content with lesser sins.
No one with an atom's weight of arrogance in his heart will enter Paradise.
Do not return after me as disbelievers striking each other's necks.
Fear Allah regarding women; I enjoin you to treat them well.
Abu Dharr insulted a man for his black mother and the Prophet told him he still had jahiliyyah in him.
Your Lord is one and your father is one; no Arab has superiority over a non-Arab except by taqwa.
I will be waiting for you at the Basin.
Let the present convey to the absent, for perhaps the one informed understands better than the one who heard.
You will be asked about me, so what will you say? They said: you conveyed and advised; he said, O Allah, bear witness.

vObke0sKS5Q.speaker_note: single voice; says this is his tenth time teaching the seerah (six in Syria, four in London) and mentions his village
vObke0sKS5Q.title: Saturday Seerah Halaqah: The Farewell Hajj and Sermon
vObke0sKS5Q.one_line: The Farewell Hajj three months before the Prophet's death and a paragraph-by-paragraph reading of his farewell sermon, applied to Muslims today.
vObke0sKS5Q.summary: He sets the Farewell Hajj three months before the Prophet's death: a time of explosive growth after Hudaybiyyah, a bittersweet return to the city that exiled him, and a man carrying the loss of eighteen close relatives. The verse completing the religion made Abu Bakr weep. He explains that the sermon was given in pieces many times, relayed by criers to a hundred thousand people, and walks through his own compilation of nine paragraphs. The sanctity of each person's life, wealth and dignity exceeds that of the holy day, month and land, so arrogance is itself harm. Jahiliyyah is placed under the Prophet's feet, beginning with his own family's blood claim and usury, so change starts with yourself; he laments Muslims denying women inheritance in his own village. Satan settles for small habitual sins that hollow out deeds. Do not return to fighting each other; be a force of unity. Treat women with the best character, which today includes educating daughters as seriously as sons. No race or colour is superior except by taqwa. He closes on the Basin, conveying knowledge so later learners exceed their teachers, and the Prophet's tearful request that Allah witness he had delivered the message.

outline.heading: Opening
The Prophet's final months: event-heavy moments under the magnifying glass
outline.gist: Some years pass in one session and some hours take several, because life is uneven; in critical moments of victory or loss Allah watches closely, which is why the Companions recorded even the Prophet's glances.

outline.heading: Farewell Hajj: a hundred thousand follow after sudden growth
outline.gist: Growth was slow for two decades, then exploded within two years of Hudaybiyyah; now a hundred thousand watch him as he tells them to take their rites from him, easing those who did them out of order.

outline.heading: Farewell Hajj: returning to the hometown that exiled him
outline.gist: Back in the city of his birth that he could never live in again, bound by his promise to the Ansar to live and die among them, with his house sold and his memories of Khadijah there.

outline.heading: Farewell Hajj: eighteen losses, and Safa twenty years on
outline.gist: At about 63 he had lost Khadijah, three daughters, his sons, Hamza and some eighteen close relatives, leaving only Fatimah; he stood again on Safa, where his uncle once cursed him, with a hundred thousand at his feet.

outline.heading: The completion verse: Abu Bakr hears the Prophet's obituary
outline.gist: While everyone rejoiced that the religion was complete and people entered Islam in crowds, Abu Bakr alone wept, knowing a peak is followed by decline; the Prophet told his companions he was only human and would soon answer his Lord's messenger.

outline.heading: Farewell Sermon: given many times, in nine paragraphs
outline.gist: Short enough to recite in minutes, it was delivered in parts at Arafah, on the day of sacrifice and the days after, hence its many wordings; its context-heavy parts show how practically he addressed his audience's problems.

outline.heading: Farewell Sermon: where it was given and how a hundred thousand heard it
outline.gist: On the Mount of Mercy or at the site of Masjid Namirah, likely both; criers on horseback relayed each line so it took hours; he works from his own compilation authenticated years ago.

outline.heading: Farewell Sermon opening: 'I may not meet you after this year'
outline.gist: He begins knowing it is the last time, which should make anyone pause; the crowd fell so still it was as if birds sat on their heads.

outline.heading: Farewell Sermon, paragraph one: what day, month and land is this?
outline.gist: He asks three times about the day, the month and the land and declares each haram, meaning sacred; this paragraph appears in every narration.

outline.heading: Farewell Sermon, paragraph one: your blood, wealth and honour are sacred
outline.gist: The sanctity of each person exceeds the holy day, month and land together; even a parent may not harm a child; his 'have I conveyed?' leaves no excuse for those who later harm each other.

outline.heading: Farewell Sermon, paragraph one: no room for arrogance
outline.gist: If others are sacred to you, arrogance and condescension are themselves harm; honour includes dignity and self-worth, so we do not dismiss or shove people aside.

outline.heading: Farewell Sermon, paragraph one: the person beside you is more sacred than Arafah
outline.gist: Groups at his Arafah day reflection read the paragraph as being about sacred places and missed it; stack every holiness together and the human beside you still outweighs it.

outline.heading: Farewell Sermon, paragraph two: jahiliyyah under his feet
outline.gist: Everything of the age of ignorance is placed under his feet so the ummah can stop reliving a past no one can fully sort out and move forward.

outline.heading: Farewell Sermon, paragraph two: his own family's blood claim and usury go first
outline.gist: Arab blood feuds ran for decades; the first claim he cancels is for a young relative killed by Hudhayl, and the first usury cancelled is his uncle al-Abbas's.

outline.heading: Farewell Sermon, paragraph two: change starts with yourself
outline.gist: Instead of complaining about Muslims, begin with your own improvement as he began with his own family, which moved others to give up their claims.

outline.heading: Farewell Sermon, paragraph two: back to jahiliyyah over women's inheritance
outline.gist: Muslims slid back into what he abolished; in his own village around 2000 about half the families pressured daughters in public to hand their inheritance to their brothers.

outline.heading: Farewell Sermon, paragraph two: put old quarrels under our feet
outline.gist: Centuries-old disputes within the ummah should be dropped as the first generations swallowed their pride; those who could not left after his death, leading to the wars of apostasy.

outline.heading: Farewell Sermon, paragraph three: Satan settles for small sins
outline.gist: Satan has despaired of idol worship in that land but is content with sins you think minor, and with a little showing off, vanity or jealousy that keeps intentions from being fully for Allah.

outline.heading: Farewell Sermon, paragraph three: deeds emptied of reward
outline.gist: Habitual small sins can void the reward of good deeds; between doing a deed and its reward lies Allah's acceptance, which no one is guaranteed.

outline.heading: Farewell Sermon, paragraph three: Satan's patience
outline.gist: He leaves you with a careless glance for fifteen years, then pushes a little further, until you fall into a major sin.

outline.heading: Farewell Sermon, paragraph four: time as Allah created it and the sacred months
outline.gist: The calendar and the four sacred months are as Allah set them when He created time, so Muslims follow authentic teachings, and people must not wrong each other in those months.

outline.heading: Farewell Sermon, paragraph four: do not return as armed enemies
outline.gist: Kuffar here comes from the root of covering, used for armour-clad fighters, so he warns against turning on each other after him, the Arabs' oldest problem.

outline.heading: Farewell Sermon, paragraph four: uniting a region never united
outline.gist: Orientalists reduce him to a general or social reformer because he united Arabs who could not even unite to defend the Kaaba.

outline.heading: Farewell Sermon, paragraph four: be a force of unity
outline.gist: The best Muslim brings people together as he did, getting the Ansar to open their homes to the Muhajirun for years; never add to the ummah's divisions.

outline.heading: Farewell Sermon, paragraph five: women are a trust from Allah
outline.gist: One of nine final paragraphs is on women's rights: men do not own their wives, who are a trust and covenant from Allah, and must treat them with the best character.

outline.heading: Farewell Sermon, paragraph five: admitting the regression
outline.gist: The duty covers every woman in a man's life; pretending all is well digs the hole deeper, and today the failure includes caring more about sons' Quran and religious education than daughters'.

outline.heading: Farewell Sermon, paragraph five: mothers raise the next generation
outline.gist: Fathers mostly regulate while mothers raise children, so without Islamically educated, supported mothers there is no hope; he returned to this theme in his later talks.

outline.heading: Farewell Sermon, paragraph six: equality proclaimed to his largest audience
outline.gist: No statement of human equality matches it; every leader, good or bad, is a strong speaker, but these simple words, said on the Mount of Mercy, should be memorized and shared.

outline.heading: Farewell Sermon, paragraph six: one Lord, one father, superiority only by taqwa
outline.gist: No Arab over non-Arab or colour over colour, the colours varying across narrations; only taqwa, which is invisible and scored by Allah alone, ranks people.

outline.heading: Farewell Sermon, paragraph six: gentle with mistakes, firm against racism
outline.gist: He was gentle with the bedouin who urinated in the masjid and the man who choked him for money, but told Abu Dharr he had jahiliyyah in him for insulting Bilal and called tribal rallying cries rotten.

outline.heading: Farewell Sermon, paragraph seven: our appointment at the Basin
outline.gist: Do your work and meet him at the Basin; some will be driven away for what they changed after him, and he asks us not to shame him before the nations through neglected dawah and children.

outline.heading: Interlude
Farewell Sermon, paragraph eight: inheritance and lineage
outline.gist: Two problems of the time, one still with us: take only your rightful inheritance and claim no lineage that is not yours.

outline.heading: Farewell Sermon, paragraph nine: let the present convey to the absent
outline.gist: Those present must pass it on, since many who receive a message understand it better than the one who heard it.

outline.heading: Farewell Sermon, paragraph nine: teach so students surpass you
outline.gist: No one can surpass the Companions in standing, but later generations can understand more; teaching succeeds only when students exceed their teachers, as our forebears hoped.

outline.heading: Farewell Sermon close: 'You will be asked about me'
outline.gist: The crowd, briefly confused, testified that he conveyed and advised; with tears he asked Allah to bear witness, leaving the rest to us.

outline.heading: Interlude
Farewell Sermon: read it yourself
outline.gist: Recite the nine paragraphs yourself at least once or twice; you may understand it more deeply than the one who teaches it, which is the point of teaching.

outline.heading: Farewell Sermon close: he gave everything and still asked for testimony
outline.gist: At 62, with no possessions and his shield in pawn, having lost his family and his city, he still wanted to know he had done enough; we should ask what people will say about us.

ioQWjgvKTDE.title: Reflections on the Farewell Sermon and the Rituals of Hajj
ioQWjgvKTDE.one_line: Why pilgrims stone the jamarat: Adam's and Ibrahim's encounters with Shaytan, submission to Allah's command, and holding to the perfected religion.
ioQWjgvKTDE.summary: Delivered in the days of tashreeq, the khutbah starts from the verse on the perfection of religion revealed at Arafah and from the pilgrims stoning the jamarat that very day. Hajj, he says, is a journey of symbolism, and without understanding it pilgrims return unchanged. He tells two stories behind the stoning. Adam and Hawwa, new to having a will, slipped, lost everything and wandered until a moment of clarity at Arafah about who they were and what they hoped for; when Shaytan returned to tempt Adam again near Mina, Adam drove him off with pebbles. Centuries later Ibrahim, a man famous for questioning, was commanded in a dream to slaughter his only son and did not question it; father, son and Hajar each threw stones at Shaytan as he tried to argue them out of obedience. The lesson of the Eid sacrifice is that Allah never commanded anything against our interest, though we owe Him everything. Seven small stones signify continuity: Shaytan never stops, so resistance must be lifelong, and everyone will orbit some centre, so make it Allah. The second khutbah quotes the Farewell Sermon on the Basin and those who deviate, and warns against compromising a religion Allah already perfected; ijtihad only applies rulings to new contexts.

outline.heading: Opening
The perfected religion, revealed at Arafah
outline.gist: The verse completing the religion came on a Friday like this one while the Prophet stood at Arafah, a sign that his mission was done and his death near; today the pilgrims are throwing the jamarat.

outline.heading: Why throw the jamarat?
outline.gist: As Hajj ends, the stoning is the ritual that takes the most time, three days in Mina for perhaps an hour and a half of throwing; so why do pilgrims do it?

outline.heading: Hajj is a journey of symbolism
outline.gist: Without the symbolism it makes little sense; countless people have gone and come back without grasping what they were part of. The stories of Adam, even in Jannah, are tied to Hajj.

outline.heading: Adam and Hawwa: new to having a will
outline.gist: They were new to having a soul, following commands and relating to Allah; Shaytan offered an upgrade from mortal to immortal, and the fear of death made the illusion work.

outline.heading: They lost everything
outline.gist: Not yet knowing how to strive against the self, they slipped; everything was stripped away in a second and they wandered, lost physically or in not knowing how to fix it, until a moment of clarity.

outline.heading: Arafah: where Adam came to know
outline.gist: The place is named for knowing: there he learned why he was created, what it meant to be khalifah and father of all humanity, and Allah showed him his descendants.

outline.heading: Hoping for Jannah: why pilgrims walk the route
outline.gist: Asked what they hoped for, they said Jannah; pilgrims walk that road every year to immortalise the moment. Then Adam sets out from Mina toward the land Allah sent him to.

outline.heading: Shaytan, unseen, and his challenge over Adam
outline.gist: Jinn are unseen to us, whatever YouTube videos claim; only prophets are in touch with that realm. Shaytan rejected the rank Allah gave Adam, who had done nothing yet but carried potential.

outline.heading: Shaytan feels he is losing
outline.gist: He proved his point by getting them to do the one thing forbidden, which is far more than eating an apple; once they repented and changed course, he came back to make Adam disobey again.

outline.heading: Adam's pebbles, and a story with its own day
outline.gist: Adam threw six or seven pebbles at the whisperer and went on to lay the Kaaba's foundations. The second story is one we are obliged to reflect on one day each year, now reduced to paying for an udhiyah delivered to the door.

outline.heading: Ibrahim's dream
outline.gist: Slaughter a hady and think of what Ibrahim saw: while being taught Hajj he dreamt of slaughtering his only son, born after long waiting, old enough to help and devoted to Allah.

outline.heading: The dream returns; the son's answer
outline.gist: Ibrahim waited in case the first dream was from Iblis; when it recurred he asked his son, who said do as commanded, you will find me patient.

outline.heading: Full submission and the silent walk
outline.gist: Not accepting Islam but surrendering their own will; he laid his son on his forehead. Imagine the silent walk of father, mother and son toward the place, and go walk it yourself.

outline.heading: A command that made no sense to a man of logic
outline.gist: Ibrahim questioned everything, which is why he became the father of prophets; to be told to kill an innocent, believing only son is worse than any harm to oneself, as every parent knows.

outline.heading: We are owed nothing
outline.gist: There was no wisdom in the act itself, which is why it never happened; the lesson to all after him is to obey, since we are owed nothing and owe Him everything, and wisdom lies in every command.

outline.heading: This time he did not question
outline.gist: The same Ibrahim once asked to see how Allah gives life so his heart would be at rest; here he understood the test, laid his son down and struck, and the knife did not cut.

outline.heading: You have fulfilled the vision
outline.gist: Like the fire that did not burn and the sea that parted, it did not happen; Allah declares the vision fulfilled and says Ibrahim was tested and completed it. What were the three thinking on that walk?

outline.heading: Shaytan's three attempts
outline.gist: A command that feels impossible breeds a million righteous objections, and Shaytan exploits it: he comes to Ibrahim, then Ismail, then Hajar, and each throws seven pebbles at him.

outline.heading: The ram: never commanded what harms you
outline.gist: A ram is slaughtered instead; each Eid we sacrifice to remember He never commanded anything not in our interest, though He could have, and we would still owe obedience.

outline.heading: Ibrahim did it anyway
outline.gist: We know His commands serve us and still do not follow; Ibrahim said bismillah and went through with it. That is how a Muslim acts, and Eid is the reminder.

outline.heading: Seven: the symbol of continuity
outline.gist: The stones are small, not boulders; in Arabic usage seven signals continuity, like the week that starts over. It is not one big blow but a fight that never ends, because he never leaves you alone.

outline.heading: Seventy stones in all
outline.gist: He works through whims, arrogance, vanity, envy, indifference, hatred and selfishness, so you must keep fighting; three jamarat over three days plus the first day comes to seventy, seven again.

outline.heading: A centre, a goal, an enemy: choose them rightly
outline.gist: You will orbit some centre, work toward some goal and fight something all your life; make the centre Allah and the enemy Shaytan, because he will never stop.

outline.heading: Interlude
The Farewell Sermon: waiting at the Basin
outline.gist: The Prophet will wait at the Basin, hoping to show the numbers who followed him, but some will be pulled away, and he will be told he does not know how they deviated after him.

outline.heading: A perfected religion: ijtihad, not new values
outline.gist: Allah perfected the deen, so we seek only better insight into what the Prophet said and did; ijtihad never changes the religion, it understands a ruling within the current context so it keeps serving its purpose.

outline.heading: Do not sell out the basics
outline.gist: Shaytan will try to make people compromise and claim right and wrong are unclear, but the Prophet explained them; Hajj takes us back to those basics.
